content: The integration of Morbidity Management and Disability Prevention (MMDP) into health services, as recommended by the Group A commitment, must be explicitly stated in the dossier. Surveillance data should be reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). If these data indicate a resurgence of infection above elimination thresholds, WHO should be consulted to determine an appropriate response. A resurgence above the original elimination target thresholds will be reflected by a change in endemicity status in the Global Health Observatory and the Weekly Epidemiological Record. Once the Director-General has acknowledged the elimination of lymphatic filariasis (LF) as a public health problem, and with the agreement of the Member State, the dossier may be made available on the WHO website as a reference document. Countries may later request verification of the elimination of transmission if appropriate evidence, amended to the dossier, demonstrates that this has occurred. Specific requirements for such verification have not yet been agreed upon. The validation of LF elimination as a public health problem involves five key steps. Validation is the process of documenting the elimination of LF as a public health problem through a validation dossier and receiving approval for the achievement from WHO. Validation is not a permanent state and does not signify the end of program activities. While some activities, such as mass drug administration (MDA), may no longer be required, programs should continue post-validation surveillance and ensure the availability of the minimum package of care for patients within the healthcare system. Elimination as a public health problem is defined as achieving specific and measurable targets for infection and disease set by WHO. Continued actions are required to maintain this status, including surveillance to ensure infection remains below target thresholds and to verify the interruption of transmission. In practice, elimination of LF as a public health problem is defined by achieving less than 1% microfilaraemia or less than 2% antigenaemia among populations aged over five years in sentinel and spot-check sites considered high-risk (Pre-TAS). All endemic areas must pass the Transmission Assessment Survey (TAS), with the number of positive children below the critical cut-off value indicating infection is below elimination thresholds, and MDA must be stopped. Infection must remain below these levels for at least four years after MDA has ceased. A successful TAS conducted more than four years after MDA meets the criteria. Target thresholds measured during TAS vary by species: Wuchereria bancrofti: <2% antigenaemia (ICT/FTS) Anopheles/Culex vector: <1% antigenaemia (ICT/FTS) Aedes vector Brugia spp.: <2% antibody (Brugia Rapid) The minimum package of care for lymphoedema and hydrocele patients must be available within the primary care system in all areas with known patients. This includes surgery to correct hydrocele, management of lymphoedema (health workers providing and teaching self-care measures such as hygiene, skin and wound care, elevation, and exercise), and treatment for acute attacks (antibiotic treatment and symptomatic management). The validation dossier contains all evidence to support the claim of achieving elimination criteria. It enables WHO to validate a country’s claim of LF elimination as a public health problem and provide feedback on necessary actions to receive WHO approval. Validation is recognized nationally based on a review of a national dossier, which requires a district-by-district (or equivalent implementation unit) approach. The minimum information requested in the dossier applies at the implementation unit (IU) level. The template dossier identifies the minimum information requested from countries and serves as a guide for writing the dossier. Post-validation surveillance involves ongoing or periodic activities conducted after WHO acknowledgment of elimination as a public health problem. The objectives are to detect and respond to recrudescence or reintroduction of LF infection above elimination thresholds and to provide additional evidence to confirm the elimination of transmission. A commitment to ongoing surveillance is required at the time of dossier submission, and ideally, activities should already be in place. Such surveillance activities may continue from post-MDA ongoing surveillance. Currently, there are no standardized activities recommended by WHO for post-validation surveillance. WHO is reviewing available evidence from research studies and country experiences to develop specific post-validation surveillance guidelines. Programs must gather data to prepare the dossier. Each section of the template dossier should be addressed and supported with program data. A national LF elimination program should archive information throughout the program’s history. If such an archive is unavailable, supportive data may be sourced from Ministry/Department of Health reports, integrated NTD databases, reports submitted to WHO, publications from research projects or surveys, regional publications, activity reports from collaborating institutions, patient case reports, health facility registers, and program evaluation reports. WHO has created a dossier data annex to facilitate the presentation of program data in the dossier. IU-specific data on endemicity, MDA, TAS, and MMDP can be entered into the annex. The template dossier was designed to help managers of national LF programs prepare a dossier with supporting evidence for presentation to WHO, requesting validation that LF has been eliminated as a public health problem. The information presented in the dossier provides the context necessary to help reviewers understand program achievements and supporting epidemiological evidence. The minimum information necessary to support the claim of elimination includes: Classification of endemic and non-endemic areas with supporting data Interventions implemented to combat LF and data on these interventions (e.g., treated population, coverage) Monitoring data of conducted interventions, including microfilaraemia and/or antigenaemia at sentinel and spot-check sites Results from TAS in endemic areas Reported or estimated number of patients with lymphoedema and hydrocele Data indicating the availability and provision of the basic recommended package of care for managing patients with lymphoedema or hydrocele Commitment to post-validation surveillance The dossier should also include a summary of the demographic and economic features of the country, referencing population census data, demographic and health surveys, and other relevant documents. It should provide indicators and/or maps on poverty, development, and household access to water and sanitation in both rural and urban areas. Additionally, the dossier should describe the LF program in the country, including historical documentation of the disease, parasite species, LF vectors, and any interventions against LF prior to the launch of the current national program. It should also outline the program’s structure, goals, and objectives, as well as its integration with other health programs.
